title: Who grants the right to be honoured
source_text: Ὅρα δὲ πῶς ἀβασάνιστόν ἐστι τὸ εἰ γάρ τι καὶ ἄλλο τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις θεραπεύσεις, ἐν ᾧ ἐμφαίνεται τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ θεραπείαν χωρὶς πάσης βλάβης ἡμῶν ἡμᾶς προσάγειν ἁπαξαπλῶς τινι τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. ἀλλ᾿ ὡσπερεὶ αἰσθηθεὶς ἑαυτοῦ οὐχ ὑγιῶς εἰπόντος· εἰ γάρ τι καὶ ἄλλο τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις θεραπεύσεις, εἶτ᾿ ἐπαναλαμβάνει καὶ διόρθωσιν προσάγει τῷ λεγομένῳ ἐν τούτῳ· οὐδ᾿ ἔξεστι τιμᾶσθαι οὐδενὶ, ὅτῳ μὴ ἐξ ἐκείνου τοῦτο δέδοται. καὶ πυθώμεθα τοῦ Κέλσου περὶ τῶν τιμωμένων ὡς θεῶν ἢ δαιμόνων ἢ καὶ ἡρώων ὅτι πόθεν, ὦ οὗτος, ἀποδεικνύναι ἔχεις ὅτι ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τούτοις δέδοται τὸ τιμᾶσθαι καὶ οὐχὶ ἀπὸ ἀγνοίας καὶ ἀμαθίας ἀνθρωπίνης πλανωμένων καὶ ἀποπιπτόντων τοῦ κυρίως τιμωμένου; τιμᾶται γοῦν, ὡς πρὸ βραχέος ἔλεγες, ὦ Κέλσε, τὰ Ἀδριανοῦ παιδικὰ, καὶ οὐ δή που ἐρεῖς ὅτι ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων δέδοται τὸ τιμᾶσθαι ὡς θεῷ τῷ Ἀντινόῳ. τὸ δ᾿ αὐτὸ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐροῦμεν. ἀπαιτοῦντες ἀπόδειξιν περὶ τοῦ δεδόσθαι αὐτοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ τὸ τιμᾶσθαι. ἐὰν δ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀνθυποφέρῃ τὸ παραπλήσιον περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ἀποδείξομεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ δέδοται αὐτῷ τὸ τιμᾶσθαι· „ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν, καθὼς τιμῶσι τὸν πατέρα.“ αἱ γὰρ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως αὐτοῦ προφητεῖαι συστάσεις ἦσαν τῆς τιμῆς αὐτοῦ. ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γενόμενα παράδοξα οὐ μαγγανείᾳ, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος, ἀλλὰ θειότητι προειρημένῃ ὑπὸ τῶν προφητῶν τὴν ἀπὸ θεοῦ εἶχε μαρτυρίαν· ἵν᾿ ὁ „τιμῶν τὸν υἱὸν“ ὄντα λόγον μηδὲν ἄλογον πράττων ὠφελῆται ἐκ τοῦ τιμᾶν αὐτὸν. καὶ τιμῶν αὐτὸν ὄντα ἀλήθειαν κρείττων γίνηται ἀπὸ τοῦ τιμᾶν ἀλήθειαν, οὕτως δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ τιμᾶν σοφίαν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καὶ πάντα, ἅπερ φασὶν εἶναι οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: See (ὅρα) how unexamined (ἀβασάνιστον) is the [phrase] 'for if you will serve/worship (θεραπεύσεις) anything else of the things in the universe (ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις)', in which it is made to appear (ἐμφαίνεται) that the worship (θεραπεία) of God brings (προσάγειν) us, without any harm (βλάβη) of ours, simply/indiscriminately (ἁπαξαπλῶς) to any one of the things of God. But as if having perceived himself not soundly (οὐχ ὑγιῶς) having said 'for if you will serve anything else of the things in the universe', then he takes it up again (ἐπαναλαμβάνει) and applies a correction (διόρθωσις) to what is said, in this: 'nor is it permitted (ἔξεστι) for anyone to be honoured (τιμᾶσθαι) to whom this has not been given (δέδοται) from Him (ἐξ ἐκείνου).' And let us inquire (πυθώμεθα) of Celsus about those honoured as gods or daemons (δαιμόνων) or even heroes (ἡρώων): whence, O you, can you demonstrate (ἀποδεικνύναι) that being honoured has been given to these from God, and not from ignorance (ἄγνοια) and want of learning (ἀμαθία) of human beings wandering (πλανωμένων) and falling away (ἀποπιπτόντων) from the one properly (κυρίως) honoured? Indeed is honoured, as a little before you were saying, O Celsus, Hadrian's boy-favourite (τὰ Ἀδριανοῦ παιδικά), and surely you will not say that from the God of the universe (τῶν ὅλων) being honoured as a god has been given to Antinous. The same we shall say also about the others, demanding proof (ἀπόδειξις) about its having been given to them from the God over all (ἐπὶ πᾶσι) to be honoured. But if he raises in turn against us (ἀνθυποφέρῃ) the similar thing about Jesus, we shall demonstrate that from God it has been given to Him to be honoured: 'that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.' For the prophecies before His birth (γένεσις) were commendations/credentials (συστάσεις) of His honour. But also the wonders (παράδοξα) done by Him, not by sorcery (μαγγανείᾳ) as Celsus thinks, but by divinity (θειότητι) foretold by the prophets, had the testimony (μαρτυρία) from God; so that the one 'honouring the Son', being Word/Reason (λόγον), doing nothing irrational (ἄλογον), may be benefited (ὠφελῆται) from honouring Him; and honouring Him being Truth (ἀλήθεια) may become better (κρείττων) from honouring truth, and so also from honouring wisdom (σοφία) and righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) and all the things which the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) say the Son of God is.
pass_b_english: See how ill-considered are the words “For if you also worship anything else in the universe”, which imply that the worship of God carries us on, without any harm to ourselves, to any one of the things that belong to God, without distinction. But as if he had noticed that he had not spoken soundly in saying “For if you also worship anything else in the universe”, he takes the point up again and corrects his statement with these words: “Nor may anyone be honoured to whom this has not been granted by Him.”

So let us ask Celsus about those who are honoured as gods, or demons, or even heroes: On what grounds, my good man, can you prove that the right to be honoured was granted to them by God, and not by the ignorance and want of learning of human beings who wander and fall away from the One to whom honour properly belongs? Hadrian’s favourite, at any rate, is honoured, as you said a little while ago, Celsus; and surely you will not say that it was the God of the universe who granted Antinous the right to be honoured as a god. We will say the same about the others too, and demand proof that the right to be honoured was granted to them by the God who is over all.

But if he turns a similar objection back on us concerning Jesus, we will show that it was from God that the right to be honoured was granted to Him: “that all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23). For the prophecies made before His birth were the credentials of His honour. And the wonders He worked, not by sorcery, as Celsus supposes, but by a divine power foretold by the prophets, had their testimony from God, so that whoever “honours the Son” (John 5:23), who is the Word, does nothing contrary to reason and may be benefited by honouring Him; and that, honouring Him who is the Truth (John 14:6), he may become better through honouring truth, and in the same way through honouring wisdom and righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and all the things that the divine Scriptures say the Son of God is.

choices.choice: Celsus’s phrases are quoted from his argument begun in 8.2 and 8.7. θεραπεύω is rendered ‘worship’ throughout this chunk; τιμάω ‘honour’. ‘Carries us on ... to any one of the things that belong to God, without distinction’ renders προσάγειν ἁπαξαπλῶς τινι τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. δαιμόνων is rendered ‘demons’, as in 8.2 and 8.7. ‘As you said a little while ago’: the Greek has πρὸ βραχέος, although Celsus’s remark about Antinous is discussed in Book 3 (3.36); kept as the Greek has it. ‘Hadrian’s favourite’ renders τὰ Ἀδριανοῦ παιδικά (his boy-beloved); the plain sense is kept without enlargement. ‘Divine power’ renders θειότητι (divinity, divine nature). In ‘the Word, does nothing contrary to reason’ Origen plays on λόγος / ἄλογον; the pun cannot be kept in English. ‘The Truth’ alludes to John 14:6; ‘wisdom and righteousness’ to 1 Corinthians 1:30. ‘The divine Scriptures’ renders οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι (the divine words).
'how carelessly he has framed the words' -> 'how ill-considered are the words' (ἀβασάνιστον, no added agency)
'to worship simply any one of the things' -> 'carries us on ... to any one of the things ... without distinction' (προσάγειν ἁπαξαπλῶς; removed added verb 'worship')
'Where ... can you prove' -> 'On what grounds ... can you prove' (πόθεν)
'who have gone astray and fallen away from the One who is truly to be honoured' -> 'who wander and fall away from the One to whom honour properly belongs' (present participles; κυρίως)
removed doubled 'worked, done' in the wonders clause
'may do nothing contrary to reason' -> 'does nothing contrary to reason' (participle πράττων, not a purpose verb)

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
